title: Simple and accessible methods for quantifying isolated mucins for further evaluation
author: McIntire-Ray, Rose, et al.
materials: The source of mucus collection is critical to determine the types of mucins present and the specific processing steps required prior for isolation. For example, a collection of sputum will primarily contain MUC5B and MUC5AC, with lesser amounts of MUC7 and the tethered mucins MUC16, MUC4, MUC1, and MUC20. On the other hand, a collection of saliva will primarily contain MUC5B with smaller amounts of MUC7 and potentially trace amounts of MUC19, MUC1, and MUC4 [1,[16], [17], [18]]. Mucus collections containing a mixture of soluble and insoluble mucins, as mentioned, may require the addition of chaotropic and/or reducing agents [19,20]. Furthermore, depending on the outcome measures, mucins can be isolated in a native state or under denatured conditions. Native conditions may be preferred if tertiary/quaternary structure, protein interactions, and/or ionic interactions are being studied [15,21]. For this purpose, we natively isolated the soluble portion of salivary MUC5B, using a slightly modified protocol based on previous established methods [15,21,22]. In the case of saliva, as outlined in the methods below, IRB approval is needed and samples should be treated as biohazard. Please follow all institutional policies related to working with saliva and make special note if potentially infectious or contaminated with blood as this is considered biohazardous.

Blotting Electric Transfer
1.Prepare 1X Tris/Glycine Buffer (as instructed by Bio-Rad) for transfer buffer.2.Soak 0.45µm nitrocellulose in Tris/Glycine Buffer.Note: This method has also been conducted with the use of 0.45µm PVDF where the addition of a 10-minute activation in methanol will be needed.3.Place gel tank in an ice bath and fill with Tris/Glycine Buffer.4.Assemble blotting sandwich in Tris/Glycine Buffer.5.Load sandwich into the mini trans-blot rig into a cooled, gel tank.6.Run the transfer at 40 V for 6-hours.7.Remove membrane, cut to size, and prepare for probing methods.

steps.title: Collect stimulated saliva
steps.instruction: Chew a piece of Parafilm and expect saliva into a 50 mL conical tube kept on ice; collect ~3.3 mL per preparation (do not swallow the Parafilm).

steps.title: Clarify saliva by centrifugation
steps.instruction: Place the tube in a refrigerated centrifuge set to 4 °C and spin at 3000 × g for 30 min; carefully decant the supernatant into a new tube and dispose of the pellet according to biohazard guidelines.

steps.title: Add solubilization buffer with inhibitors
steps.instruction: Add Solubilization Buffer (pH 7.4) containing EDTA‑free protease inhibitor cocktail to the clarified saliva at a 2 : 1 buffer‑to‑saliva volume ratio (e.g., bring total volume to ~10 mL if less than 3.3 mL saliva was collected).

steps.title: Incubate on rotator overnight
steps.instruction: Place the tube on a rotator and incubate at 4 °C for ~16 h (overnight).

steps.title: Second centrifugation
steps.instruction: Centrifuge the overnight‑rotated sample in a pre‑cooled 4 °C centrifuge at 4400 × g for 30 min.

steps.title: Collect clarified supernatant
steps.instruction: Transfer the supernatant to a fresh tube; this will be used for the isopycnic CsCl gradient.

substeps.instruction: Pre‑weigh an empty 0.2 mL tube on a microbalance.
Add 200 µL of the fraction to the tube.
Allow the sample to equilibrate to room temperature, then weigh again.
Record the net weight, return the sample to its original fraction tube, and keep the tube on ice when not weighing.
Multiply the recorded weight by 5 to convert to mg mL⁻¹ (since 200 µL × 5 = 1 mL).
Plot the calculated density (mg mL⁻¹) versus fraction number; expect densities centering around 1.45 mg mL⁻¹ for a 1.45 mg mL⁻¹ CsCl starting density, with a monotonic increase from fraction 1 to 24.

steps.title: Assess fractions for mucin content
steps.instruction: Measure each fraction’s absorbance at 280 nm using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer to identify non‑mucin proteins/DNA; perform MUC5B slot‑blot immunoblotting and/or dot‑blot followed by Periodic‑Acid‑Schiff (PAS) staining to locate mucin‑containing fractions (typically fractions 11–20).

substeps.instruction: For PAS staining, treat the membrane with 1 % (v/v) periodic acid, 3 % (v/v) acetic acid, wash, incubate in 0.1 % (w/v) sodium metabisulfite, 10 mM HCl, then apply Schiff’s reagent.
Develop the blot and visualize magenta‑stained mucin bands.

steps.title: Pool mucin‑rich fractions and exchange buffer
steps.instruction: Combine the identified mucin‑containing fractions, then perform a buffer exchange into Storage Buffer (10 mM Tris, 10 mM NaCl, pH 7.4; optionally add 0.05 % NaN₃).

steps.title: Prepare sample for Ag‑PAGE
steps.instruction: Process the pooled mucin sample as follows:

substeps.instruction: Load the sample onto a 10 kDa centrifugal filter unit.
Exchange the Storage Buffer for Reduction Buffer (pH 8.0) using the same filter.
Adjust the volume to achieve a final concentration of 400 µg mL⁻¹.
Add 10 mM DTT and incubate in a 37 °C water bath for 5 h.
Remove from the bath, add 20 mM iodoacetamide, and cover the tube; let sit at room temperature overnight.
Add 10X Sample Loading Buffer (containing 1 % SDS, 50 % glycerol, 0.01 % bromophenol blue, etc.) and incubate 10 min before loading onto the gel.
Place the Mini‑PROTEAN Tetra Cell casting assembly, gel combs, glass spacers, and a 25 mL serological pipette in a 65 °C oven for 45–60 min.
Keep the Polyacrylamide Solution (without TEMED/APS) warm in the oven.
In a 125 mL Erlenmeyer flask, dilute 1X Gel Buffer and add 1 % (w/v) agarose; hydrate for 20 min then microwave gently until fully dissolved.
Add 0.15 % (v/v) TEMED and 0.07 % (w/v) APS to the warmed Polyacrylamide Solution and mix by inversion.
Combine the agarose solution with the 1.5 % polyacrylamide solution, swirling gently.
Pour the agarose‑polyacrylamide mixture into the heated casting apparatus, avoiding bubbles.
Insert the gel combs, allow the gel to cure at room temperature for 1 h, then store at 4 °C overnight (or up to 2 weeks).
Prepare 1X Running Buffer (10 mM Trizma Base, 10 mM EDTA, 1 % SDS, 1.92 M Trizma Base, 0.45 % boric acid) and adjust pH to 8.0; add ~20.5 g boric acid to achieve the correct pH.
Place the cured gels into the 4‑gel vertical electrophoresis system and fill the chambers with Running Buffer.
Load each well with 25 µL of sample at 400 µg mL⁻¹ (multiple dilutions may be loaded).
Run at 60 V until the dye front exits the gel (~3.5 h). Optionally increase to 80 V for an additional 15–30 min to enhance migration.
Prepare 1X Tris/Glycine transfer buffer as per Bio‑Rad instructions.
Soak a 0.45 µm nitrocellulose membrane in the buffer (PVDF can be used with a 10‑min methanol activation).
Place the gel tank in an ice bath and fill with transfer buffer.
Assemble the blotting sandwich (gel, membrane, filter papers, sponges) in transfer buffer.
Insert the sandwich into the Mini‑Trans‑Blot rig and run at 40 V for 6 h.
Remove the membrane, cut to desired size, and proceed to probing.

steps.title: Probe membrane for mucin
steps.instruction: Detect MUC5B on the transferred membrane:

substeps.instruction: Block the membrane with 5 % non‑fat dry milk in TBS‑T (0.1 % Tween‑20).
Incubate with primary anti‑MUC5B antibody (NovusBio, #4A10‑H2) diluted in blocking buffer.
Wash and incubate with IRDye 680RD goat anti‑mouse IgG secondary antibody (Li‑Cor, #926‑68070).
Image the blot using a Li‑Cor Odyssey M system.

steps.title: Quantify mucin by Bradford assay
steps.instruction: Determine mucin concentration using a Mucin Bradford assay:

substeps.instruction: Prepare a standard curve with Bovine Submaxillary Mucin (BSM) and BSA for comparison.
Add Bradford reagent to aliquots of the pooled mucin sample and standards; measure absorbance at 595 nm.
Calculate the mucin concentration from the BSM standard curve (preferred over BSA).
